## Introduction & Epidemiology {.smaller}

- Cystic neoplasms have become a well-defined radiographic entity
- **Estimated incidence:** 2.6 cystic lesions per 100 individuals per year
- Detection rates vary by modality:
  - Abdominal US: **0.21%**
  - CT: **2.6%**
  - MRI/MRCP: **2.4% – 49.1%**
  - Autopsy studies: up to **50%**

::: {.callout}
The diagnosis rate has increased due to better imaging quality, increased cross-sectional imaging use, and an aging population.
:::

---

## Classification (WHO) {.smaller}

- **Neoplastic cysts**
  - **Mucin-producing:** IPMNs, MCNs
  - **Non-mucin producing:** SCAs, SPTs
- **Non-neoplastic cysts**
  - Pseudocysts (no epithelial lining)
- Mucinous cysts = **malignant precursor lesions**
  - Lined by endoderm-derived columnar epithelium
- Non-mucinous cysts = generally benign
  - Lined by simple cuboidal epithelium

::: {.callout}
Up to 20% of unexplained pancreatitis occurs because of cystic neoplasms. Pseudocysts develop in up to 50% of patients with acute pancreatitis.
:::

---

## Overview of Common Cystic Neoplasms

<div style="overflow-x:auto; font-size: 0.70em;">

| Feature | IPMN-BD | IPMN-MD | MCN | SCA | SPT |
|---------|---------|---------|-----|-----|-----|
| **Age** | 5th–7th decade | 5th–7th decade | 4th–5th decade | 5th–7th decade | 2nd–3rd decade |
| **Gender** | Equal | Equal | Female > Male | Female >> Male | Female >> Male |
| **Location** | Head/uncinate | Diffuse/segmental | Body/tail | Any | Tail/body |
| **MPD Connection** | Yes | Yes | No | No | No |
| **Malignant Potential** | 12%–30% | 36%–100% | 10%–50% | Negligible | 10%–15% |
| **Key Marker** | GNAS mut | GNAS mut | RNF43 mut | VHL mut | CTNNB1 mut |

</div>


<small>This table summarizes the key clinicopathologic variables. MCNs are distinguished by ovarian-type stroma and are almost exclusively found in females.</small>


---

## Serous Cystadenomas (SCAs) {.smaller}

- First characterized by Compagno & Oertel in **1978**
- **~50% found incidentally**
- Symptoms (when present): abdominal pain, palpable mass, weight loss, early satiety
- **Morphologic varieties:**
  - Microcystic (classic honeycomb appearance)
  - Macrocystic / oligocystic
  - Mixed
  - Solid

::: {.callout}
SCAs can be associated with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, generally diagnosed at younger age (~25 years) and have a benign course.
:::

---

## SCAs: Imaging & Pathology {.smaller}

- **Pathognomonic finding:** Central "stellate scar" with or without calcification
- Septations and thick fibrous walls with innumerable small cysts
- **Macrocystic/oligocystic variants** can mimic mucinous lesions
- Solid component may be visualized due to fibrous nature — **not necessarily malignant**
- **Serous cystadenocarcinoma is extremely rare** (< 1% true incidence)
  - Only ~30 cases reported in literature
  - Even with metastasis, long-term prognosis is excellent

::: {.callout}
In a multinational study of 2622 patients with SCAs, only 0.1% had serous cystadenocarcinoma. The more common problem is local invasion causing symptoms.
:::

---

## SCAs: Management {.smaller}

::: {.callout}
Conservative Approach is Standard
:::

- Asymptomatic patients: **follow radiographically**
- Resection reserved for:
  - Symptomatic patients
  - Significant growth / large lesions
  - Diagnostic dilemma
  - Concern for invasive carcinoma (rare)
- Growth rate ~0.6 cm/year (higher in lesions >4 cm)
- **Risk of invasive carcinoma < 1%** — surgical risk exceeds cancer risk

::: {.callout}
Decisions for large SCAs should be individualized based on age, tumor location, and comorbidities. Function-preserving minimally invasive resection may be considered in young, healthy patients.
:::

---

## Mucinous Cystic Neoplasms (MCNs) {.smaller}

- **Mucin-producing cystic tumors** lacking communication with pancreatic duct
- **Pathognomonic:** Ovarian-like stroma surrounding columnar epithelium
- **Almost exclusively found in females**
- Most common in **body and tail** of pancreas
- Size range: 2 cm to 25 cm
- Often discovered incidentally; symptoms include pain, nausea, back pain, pancreatitis

::: {.callout}
Any macrocystic lesion in the distal pancreas of a female patient should be highly suspicious for MCN. May have peripheral "eggshell" calcifications.
:::

---

## MCNs: Malignant Potential & Management {.smaller}

- **Risk of invasive carcinoma: 10%–50%**
- Concerning features:
  - Male gender
  - Pancreatic head/neck location
  - Larger size
  - **Mural nodules**
  - Duct dilation
- **5-year disease-specific survival with invasive carcinoma:** 57%–64%

::: {.callout}
<div class="callout-title">Treatment Recommendations</div>
- **IAP 2012:** Resection for all MCNs regardless of size
- **European 2018:** Resection if ≥4 cm, mural nodules, or symptoms
- Small asymptomatic MCNs (<4 cm) may be followed every 6 months
:::

::: {.callout}
No surveillance needed after resection of noninvasive MCN — unlike IPMN, there is no lifelong follow-up required. This favors resection in young patients.
:::

---

## Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms (IPMNs) {.smaller}

- Epithelial tumors arising from main or branch pancreatic ducts
- Cause ductal dilation from **mucin production**
- Classified by **radiographic subtype:**
  - **Main-duct (MD-IPMN):** Diffuse or segmental MPD dilation >5 mm
  - **Branch-duct (BD-IPMN):** Communication with MPD without significant MPD dilation
  - **Mixed:** Both branch-duct and main-duct dilation

::: {.callout}
IPMNs represent 15%–30% of all cystic neoplasms. Peak incidence between 50–70 years. Occurs equally in men and women, unlike MCNs.
:::

---

## IPMN: Radiographic Subtypes & Risk {.smaller}

| Subtype | Malignancy Risk | Invasive Cancer |
|---------|----------------|-----------------|
| **MD-IPMN** | ~60% (HGD + invasive) | ~45% |
| **Mixed IPMN** | Intermediate | Intermediate |
| **BD-IPMN** | 12%–30% | Lower |

- **Morphologic subtypes:** Gastric, Intestinal, Pancreatobiliary, Oncocytic
- Each subtype exhibits particular risk of invasive carcinoma
- Histologic grading: **Low-grade dysplasia → High-grade dysplasia → Invasive carcinoma**

::: {.callout}
The radiographic classification forms the backbone of management. MD-IPMN generally warrants resection due to high malignant potential.
:::

---

## IPMN-Associated Cancer {.smaller}


- Invasive cancer found in **20%–50%** of resected IPMN specimens
- BD-IPMN cumulative incidence of invasive carcinoma:
  - 5 years: **3.3%**
  - 10 years: **6.6%**
  - 15 years: **15.0%**
- **Risk factors for invasive cancer**

  ::: {.columns}

  ::: {.column width="50%"}
  - Jaundice
  - Pancreatitis
  - New-onset diabetes
  - Cyst size ≥3 cm
  - Mural nodules
  :::

  ::: {.column width="50%"}
  - Main-duct dilation
  - Abrupt duct caliber change with distal atrophy
  - Elevated serum CA 19-9
  :::

  :::

::: {.callout}
Patients with IPMN also have 1%–8% risk of developing conventional pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma elsewhere in the pancreas.
:::


---

## Prognosis of IPMN-Associated Cancer {.smaller}


- **5-year survival:** 43%–60% (better than conventional ductal adenocarcinoma at ~15%)
- Improved outcome likely due to **earlier stage at resection**
- **Colloid subtype** has significantly better survival than tubular subtype
- **Negative prognostic factors:**
  - Tubular-variant histology
  - Lymph node involvement
  - Perineural/vascular invasion
  - Positive margins


::: {.callout}
If adverse tumor factors are present, outcome is similar to conventional ductal adenocarcinoma. The survival advantage is primarily stage-related.
:::

---

## Genetics of IPMN {.smaller}

- **Shared mutations with pancreatic cancer:**
  - KRAS mutations
  - Loss of p16
  - TP53 mutations
- **Key differences from pancreatic cancer:**
  - **SMAD4/DPC4 preserved** in virtually all noninvasive IPMNs
  - **GNAS mutations** in up to 66% of IPMNs — **not found** in other cyst types or non-IPMN adenocarcinomas
- **Mutation patterns predict histology:**
  - **Colloid carcinoma:** GNAS predominant, KRAS uncommon
  - **Tubular carcinoma:** KRAS predominant, GNAS uncommon

::: {.callout}
Whole-exome sequencing shows IPMNs have alterations of RNF43, GNAS, or KRAS, and never VHL or CTNNB1. Molecular analysis improves diagnostic accuracy when combined with clinical and radiologic data.
:::

---

## Diagnostic Evaluation: Imaging {.smaller}

- **Multidetector CT:** Most common method; evaluates septations, mural nodules, calcifications
- **MRCP:** Better than CT for:
  - Duct connection
  - Enhancing mural nodules
  - Internal septations
- **Secretin-enhanced MRCP:** Improves visualization of cyst-duct communication
- Pancreatic protocol CT critical for detecting radiographically occult invasive cancer

::: {.callout}
High-quality cross-sectional imaging is the key to diagnostic evaluation. Careful visualization of the cystic lesion allows evaluation of features that predict malignancy.
:::

---

## Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) {.smaller}

- **Indicated when:**
  - Concerning clinical or radiologic features
  - Need for cyst fluid analysis
- **Contrast-enhanced EUS:** Most accurate for discriminating mural nodules vs. mucin clots
- **Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE):**
  - Real-time microscopic visualization
  - SCA: "Fern pattern" / superficial vascular network
  - MCN: Epithelial bands without papillary configuration
  - IPMN: Finger-like papillae

::: {.callout}
EUS is operator-dependent. A gastroenterologist with expertise in EUS is highly valuable. Contrast-enhanced EUS characterizes vascularity using microbubbles.
:::

---

## Cyst Fluid Analysis {.smaller}

- **CEA > 192 ng/mL:** Best predictor of mucinous lesion (79% accuracy)
  - SCAs and retention cysts: undetectable CEA
  - Cannot predict invasive disease
- **Amylase:**
  - Low levels exclude pseudocyst
  - High levels nonspecific (seen in SCAs, IPMNs, MCNs)
- **Glucose:** Potential biomarker with similar accuracy to CEA
- **Cytology:** Limited by small volume and low cellular content

::: {.callout}
A through-the-needle forceps device has been introduced for EUS-guided tissue acquisition but remains investigational.
:::

---

## Molecular Markers & CompCyst {.smaller}

- **Advanced neoplasia associated with:**
  - SMAD4, CDKN2A, TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN alterations
- **KRAS mutation + allelic loss:** Initially felt predictive of malignancy
  - Sensitivity only ~11% (high specificity)
- **Das-1 antibody:** High sensitivity/specificity for high-risk/invasive carcinoma
- **CompCyst (machine learning):**
  - Integrates clinical, imaging, and genetic data
  - More accurate than conventional criteria alone
  - Potential to reduce morbidity and costs

::: {.callout}
CompCyst analyzes mutations including KRAS, GNAS, RNF43, CDKN2A, CTNNB1, TP53, BRAF, VHL, PIK3CA to diagnose and determine management.
:::

---

## Treatment: Main-Duct IPMN {.smaller}

::: {.callout}
<div class="callout-title">Generally Recommend Resection</div>
- High risk of high-grade dysplasia or invasive disease
- Even without invasive cancer at presentation, most MD-IPMNs will progress to invasive carcinoma
:::

- **Extent of resection:**
  - Standard resection with lymphadenectomy if invasive cancer suspected
  - Partial pancreatectomy (Whipple or distal) if disease localized
  - **Intraoperative frozen section** critical for margin assessment
- **Margin management (IAP 2017):**
  - Low-grade dysplasia: No further resection
  - High-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma: Consider additional resection

::: {.callout}
Total pancreatectomy generally avoided unless diffuse gland involvement. Morbidity of total pancreatectomy is significant (59% in high-volume centers, 2.1% 30-day mortality).
:::

---

## Treatment: Mixed-Type IPMN {.smaller}

- Historically treated like MD-IPMN
- **Recent evidence:** Minimal MPD involvement ≠ same malignant potential as true MD-IPMN
- **European 2018 guidelines:**
  - MPD ≥10 mm: Absolute indication for surgery
  - MPD 5–9 mm: Relative indication
- **IAP 2017:**
  - MPD ≥10 mm: Resection
  - MPD 5–9 mm: "Worrisome feature" — EUS evaluation, not immediate surgery

::: {.callout}
During international consensus, 41% of experts advised surveillance for MPD 5–9 mm, while 59% advised operative intervention.
:::

---

## Postoperative Surveillance After IPMN Resection {.smaller}

- **IAP 2017:**
  - High-risk features (family history of pancreatic cancer, positive margin with HGD, nonintestinal subtype): Every 6 months
  - All others: Every 6–12 months
- **European 2018:**
  - HGD or main duct involvement: Every 6 months for 2 years, then yearly
  - Low-grade dysplasia: Same as nonresected IPMN
- **Completion pancreatectomy** indicated for progression thought to be HGD or invasive carcinoma

::: {.callout}
Surveillance is warranted for development of additional lesions in remnant gland (noninvasive) or distant/gland recurrence (invasive).
:::

---

## Treatment: Branch-Duct IPMN {.smaller}

::: {.callout}
<div class="callout-title">Selective Resection Based on Risk Stratification</div>
:::

- **High-risk stigmata** → Resection without further testing:
  - Obstructive jaundice + cystic head lesion
  - Enhancing mural nodule ≥5 mm
  - Main pancreatic duct ≥10 mm
- **Worrisome features** → EUS evaluation:
  - Pancreatitis, cyst ≥3 cm, mural nodule <5 mm
  - Thickened/enhancing walls, MPD 5–9 mm
  - Abrupt MPD caliber change with atrophy
  - Lymphadenopathy, elevated CA 19-9
  - Cyst growth rate >5mm/2 years

::: {.callout}
Patients with "worrisome features" had 96% 5-year disease-specific survival with conservative management. "High-risk stigmata" had 40% risk of IPMN-related death.
:::

---


## Treatment: Branch-Duct IPMN {.smaller}

::: {.callout}
<div class="callout-title">The 2018 European guidelines are broadly similar to the 2017 IAP recommendations for management of BD-IPMN.</div>
:::


:::{.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Absolute Indications for Surgery

    - Obstructive jaundice
    - Cytology positive for **high-grade dysplasia** or **cancer**
    - Contrast-enhancing mural nodule **≥ 5 mm**
    - Presence of a **solid mass**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Relative Indications for Surgery

    - Growth rate **≥ 5 mm/year**
    - Serum **CA 19-9 > 37 U/mL** (without jaundice)
    - Main pancreatic duct diameter **5-9.9 mm**
    - Cyst size **≥ 4 cm**, New-onset **diabetes mellitus or AP**
    - Contrast-enhancing mural nodules **< 5 mm**
:::
:::

Patients with relative indications should undergo **closer follow-up or resection** depending on comorbidities.



---

## BD-IPMN: Surgical Details {.smaller}

- Head lesions: **Pancreatoduodenectomy**
- Tail lesions: **Distal pancreatectomy** ± splenectomy
- **Pancreas-sparing procedures:**
  - Enucleation
  - Central pancreatectomy
  - Uncinate process resection
- Feasible in selected patients (89% feasibility in one study)
- **Higher morbidity** than standard resections (mainly pancreatic fistula)

::: {.callout}
Whether pancreas-sparing procedures preserve exocrine and endocrine function better than standard resections requires further study.
:::

---

## Solid Pseudopapillary Tumor (SPT) {.smaller}

- Also known as **Frantz or Hamoudi tumors**
- Account for ~2.5% of resected pancreatic neoplasms
- **Female:male ratio = 9:1**
- Mean age: **29 years**
- Only **38% asymptomatic** at presentation
- Common symptoms: Pain (64%), palpable mass (33%)
- Mean tumor size: **8.6 cm**
- Most common location: **Tail and body** (59%)

::: {.callout}
SPTs may present acutely with rupture and hemoperitoneum. When a well-encapsulated mass with solid and cystic components is found in a young female, SPT should top the differential.
:::

---

## SPT: Pathology & Genetics {.smaller}

- **Imaging:** Encapsulated lesions with hypodense areas (necrosis/hemorrhage)
- **Histology:** Polygonal epithelial cells in discohesive pattern
- **Immunohistochemistry:** Vimentin, keratin, NSE, CD10, progesterone positive
- **Molecular:**
  - Abnormal β-catenin expression present
  - KRAS, p53, DPC4 typically unaltered
  - Wnt/β-catenin, Hedgehog, androgen receptor pathways activated
  - Genes involved in epithelial mesenchymal transition activated

::: {.callout}
SPTs are distinct from normal pancreatic parenchyma and rarely cause ductal dilation due to lack of invasion. MRI shows high T1 signal in areas of hemorrhagic necrosis.
:::

---

## SPT: Management {.smaller}

::: {.callout}
<div class="callout-title">Generally Indolent — Cured with Complete Surgical Extirpation</div>
:::

- **Metastatic disease:** Present in up to 15%
- **"Malignant" criteria:**
  - Locally advanced disease with vascular invasion
  - Lymph node metastasis
  - Hepatic metastasis
- **Long-term survival possible** even with metastatic disease
- **Progression rate after surgery:** ~2.6% in nonmetastatic SPTs
- **Risk factors for progression:**
  - Male gender, positive lymph nodes
  - Positive margin at time of resection, lymphovascular invasion

::: {.callout}
Significant vascular invasion is the most common reason for unresectability. Resection should still be considered in selected cases with metastatic disease.
:::

---

## Conclusions {.smaller}

- Most common lesions: **IPMNs, MCNs, and SCAs**
- **No definitive strategy** exists to differentiate various cyst types
- Management requires **multidisciplinary team** with expertise in:
  - Advanced imaging
  - Endoscopy
  - Pathology
  - Surgical treatment
- **SCAs:** Benign — conservative management
- **Mucinous lesions:** Generally resect, especially if >3 cm, solid component, and ductal dilation
- **Advancements** in biomarkers and machine learning (CompCyst) improving nonoperative diagnosis

::: {.callout}
The initial evaluation of a small, benign-appearing cyst should include one early interval image to ensure no occult invasive carcinoma or high-grade dysplasia is present.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways {.smaller}

1. **SCAs:** <1% malignant risk — observe unless symptomatic
2. **MCNs:** 10%–50% malignant risk — resect (especially if ≥4 cm or symptomatic)
3. **MD-IPMN:** ~60% malignant risk — generally resect
4. **BD-IPMN:** Resect only with high-risk stigmata or worrisome features
5. **SPT:** Surgical resection curative in most; indolent even when "malignant"
6. **Molecular markers** (GNAS, KRAS, RNF43) increasingly guide diagnosis
7. **CompCyst** and advanced EUS techniques represent the future of cyst management
